question: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. Automated review runs on every push to a PR, and developers complain that each new commit produces the same comments they've already seen, alongside a few genuinely new ones. How should the review step be changed?
options: Run the review only on the first push of each PR and skip all subsequent commits.
Delete all previous review comments before posting the new set of findings.
Raise the severity threshold so that fewer, more important findings are reported on each subsequent run of the review.
Include the prior review findings in context and instruct Claude to report only new or still-unaddressed issues.
explanation:
- Option D is correct because giving the reviewer its previous findings lets it skip issues that were already reported and fixed, while still flagging regressions and unresolved items.
- Option A is incorrect because later commits can introduce new bugs that would go unreviewed.
- Option B is incorrect because it erases discussion history and re-posts the same content.
- Option C is incorrect because it suppresses legitimate findings without addressing the duplication.

question: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline for automated PR review. One review instruction reads "Check that code comments are accurate." It produces dozens of findings per PR about vague or slightly outdated wording, and developers have started ignoring the reviewer. What is the best rewrite?
options: "Check that code comments are accurate, and be conservative about what you flag."
"Only report comment issues when you are highly confident that the comment is wrong."
"Flag a comment only when the behaviour it claims contradicts what the code actually does."
"Report every comment issue, but label the minor ones as low severity so that developers can skip them."
explanation:
- Option C is correct because explicit, categorical criteria define precisely what counts as an issue, which sharply reduces false positives.
- Option A is incorrect because general instructions like "be conservative" don't improve precision; the model has no concrete threshold to apply.
- Option B is incorrect because confidence-based filtering is vague and poorly calibrated compared with specific criteria.
- Option D is incorrect because it keeps the noise, and high false positive volume erodes trust even when it is labelled.

question: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline for automated PR review. To cut noise you added "Only report high-confidence findings" to the prompt, but the false positive rate barely changed. What should you do instead?
options: Define which categories to report (bugs, security vulnerabilities) and which to skip (minor style, local patterns).
Add "Be extremely conservative and avoid false positives" in bold to the beginning of the prompt.
Ask the model to give each finding a confidence score from 1 to 10, and keep only the findings that score 9 or above.
Lower the temperature to 0 so that the reviewer produces fewer speculative findings on each run.
explanation:
- Option A is correct because specific report/skip criteria improve precision far more than confidence-based phrasing. The model knows exactly what is in and out of scope.
- Option B is incorrect because it is the same kind of general instruction that has already failed.
- Option C is incorrect because uncalibrated self-reported confidence is an unreliable filter.
- Option D is incorrect because temperature affects variability, not the model's understanding of what is worth reporting.

question: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline for automated PR review. Security and correctness findings are about 90% accurate, but "naming convention" findings are wrong about 60% of the time. Developers now dismiss all findings, including valid security issues. What should you do first?
options: Keep every category enabled and add a note to each review explaining that naming findings may be less reliable than others.
Disable the whole automated reviewer until the false positive rate for every category is below 10%.
Merge naming findings into the general findings list so that they stand out less in the review.
Temporarily disable the naming category to restore trust, while improving the prompt for that category separately.
explanation:
- Option D is correct because a high false positive category undermines confidence in accurate categories. Turning it off restores trust in the valuable findings while you fix its criteria.
- Option A is incorrect because a disclaimer doesn't stop the noise that is driving developers to dismiss everything.
- Option B is incorrect because it throws away the high-value security and correctness findings.
- Option C is incorrect because hiding the category's label leaves the noise in place and makes it harder to filter.

question: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. Your review prompt describes the required output in detail (location, issue, severity, suggested fix), yet findings arrive in inconsistent shapes: some omit the fix, and others merge several issues into one paragraph. What is the most effective improvement?
options: Repeat the output format description at both the start and the end of the review prompt.
Add a few examples of correctly formatted findings, each showing a location, issue, severity and suggested fix.
Raise max_tokens so that the model has enough room to include every field in each finding.
Ask the model to restate the required output format in its own words before it begins writing any of its findings.
explanation:
- Option B is correct because few-shot examples are the most effective technique for consistent, actionable formatting when detailed instructions alone produce inconsistent results.
- Option A is incorrect because repetition reinforces the same instructions that are already being followed inconsistently.
- Option C is incorrect because output length isn't what causes fields to be missing.
- Option D is incorrect because restating the format doesn't reliably change how the model applies it.

question: You are building a structured data extraction system that pulls citations from research papers and validates them against a JSON schema. Extraction works on papers with inline citations, but the required references field often comes back empty for papers that use a numbered bibliography at the end. What is the most effective fix?
options: Make the references field optional so that empty values no longer cause the extraction to fail schema validation.
Add a system prompt instruction that says "Always find every citation in the paper."
Add few-shot examples showing correct extraction from both inline-citation and numbered-bibliography papers.
Preprocess every paper to remove the bibliography section before it is sent for extraction.
explanation:
- Option C is correct because few-shot examples demonstrating varied document structures teach the model to handle each format, which fixes empty extractions of required fields.
- Option A is incorrect because it hides the failure; the references exist in the document and should be extracted.
- Option B is incorrect because the model already intends to find citations; it lacks a demonstration of what the other structure looks like.
- Option D is incorrect because it deletes the very information being extracted.

question: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline for automated review. To reduce false positives you wrote 15 rules, each describing a specific acceptable pattern. The reviewer handles those 15 patterns well but still flags new variants that are equally acceptable. What should you change?
options: Keep adding a new rule whenever another acceptable pattern turns up, until the list eventually covers every case.
Merge the 15 rules into one general instruction: "Only flag code that is actually problematic."
Raise the reviewer's severity threshold so that only critical findings are reported.
Add 2-4 few-shot examples of ambiguous cases, each explaining why the code is acceptable or a real issue.
explanation:
- Option D is correct because few-shot examples that show the reasoning behind a decision let the model generalize to novel patterns rather than matching only the pre-specified ones.
- Option A is incorrect because an ever-growing list can't anticipate every variant and bloats the prompt.
- Option B is incorrect because a vague instruction loses the specificity that improved precision.
- Option C is incorrect because it suppresses legitimate non-critical findings without teaching the distinction.

question: You are building a structured data extraction system for invoices. You currently ask Claude to "return the result as JSON" and parse the text response, and about 3% of responses fail to parse because of missing brackets or trailing commentary. What is the most reliable fix, and what does it not guarantee?
options: Add "Return valid JSON only, with no other text" to the prompt. This guarantees valid syntax but not that the values are correct.
Define an extraction tool whose input schema is the invoice schema. This eliminates syntax errors but not semantic ones, such as line items that don't sum to the total.
Retry any response that fails to parse until a valid one comes back. Because only parseable responses are kept, this guarantees both valid syntax and correct values.
Post-process each response with a lenient JSON repair library. This eliminates syntax errors and, because the repaired output is re-validated, also catches semantic mistakes.
explanation:
- Option B is correct because tool use with a JSON schema is the most reliable route to schema-compliant structured output and eliminates syntax errors. It doesn't prevent semantic errors, such as values in the wrong field or totals that don't add up, which need separate validation.
- Option A is incorrect because prompt instructions reduce syntax errors but don't eliminate them.
- Option C is incorrect because retries add cost, and nothing about valid syntax guarantees correct values.
- Option D is incorrect because a repair library may guess wrongly at structure and cannot detect semantic mistakes.

question: You are building a structured data extraction system. Your pipeline defines extract_metadata plus several enrichment tools, such as lookup_vendor and classify_spend. extract_metadata must always run first, because the enrichment tools depend on its output. How should you configure the first request?
options: tool_choice: "auto", with a system prompt instruction telling Claude that it must call extract_metadata first, before anything else.
tool_choice: "any", so that Claude is guaranteed to call at least one of the tools.
Remove the enrichment tools entirely and handle their work later in application code.
tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"}, then handle the enrichment steps in follow-up turns.
explanation:
- Option D is correct because forced tool selection guarantees that a specific named tool is called, ensuring extract_metadata runs before the enrichment steps that follow.
- Option A is incorrect because with "auto" the model may reply with text or choose another tool; the instruction is only probabilistic.
- Option B is incorrect because "any" guarantees some tool call, not this particular one. It suits cases where the right schema isn't known in advance.
- Option C is incorrect because it gives up model-driven enrichment unnecessarily.

question: You are building a structured data extraction system for supplier contracts. Some contracts have no termination clause, and payment terms vary widely across contracts. You have seen the model invent termination dates and squeeze unusual payment terms into the wrong category. Which TWO schema design choices address these problems? (Choose two.)
options: Make termination_date optional and nullable, so that the model can return null when the clause is absent.
Make every field required, so that the model is forced to look harder for the information.
Use a free-form string for payment_terms, so that the model can describe any arrangement it finds.
Require "N/A" as the value of any field the model cannot find in the contract.
Use an enum for payment_terms that includes "other", paired with a payment_terms_detail string field.
explanation:
- Option A is correct because nullable optional fields let the model represent missing information honestly instead of fabricating values to satisfy a required field.
- Option E is correct because an enum with "other" plus a detail string keeps categorization consistent while handling cases the enum doesn't cover.
- Option B is incorrect because forcing values for absent information is exactly what drives fabrication.
- Option C is incorrect because free-form strings give up consistent categorization for downstream systems.
- Option D is incorrect because sentinel strings are ambiguous, break type expectations, and are an inferior substitute for null.

question: You are building a structured data extraction system for invoices. Your validator finds that an extraction's line items sum to $4,310 while total_amount is $4,130. How should the retry request be constructed?
options: Send the same request again, since the model will probably produce a correct extraction next time.
Include the original document, the failed extraction and the specific error: line items sum to $4,310 but the total is $4,130.
Send only the validation error message and ask the model to correct its previous answer from memory, without resending the document.
Ask the model to re-extract the invoice and be more careful with all of the numbers this time.
explanation:
- Option B is correct because retry-with-error-feedback works best when the model has the source, its previous attempt and the precise validation failure, so it can find and fix the specific mistake.
- Option A is incorrect because blind retries ignore the information that would guide the correction.
- Option C is incorrect because API calls are stateless; without the document and the prior output the model cannot check its work.
- Option D is incorrect because a generic instruction doesn't say what is wrong.

question: You are building a structured data extraction system for supplier contracts. For one group of contracts, the renewal_date field keeps failing validation after three retries with detailed error feedback. On inspection, those contracts say "renewal terms as defined in Amendment B," and Amendment B is not part of the input. What is the right response?
options: Increase the retry limit to ten so that the model has more chances to produce a valid date.
Add few-shot examples showing how to infer renewal dates from contract language.
Make renewal_date required, with a default value of exactly one year after the contract's signing date when no date is found.
Accept that retries can't recover absent information: return null and route the contracts for Amendment B to be supplied.
explanation:
- Option D is correct because retries fix format and structural errors, not missing information. When the data exists only in an external document that wasn't provided, more retries just burn cost, and the right outcome is null plus a route to obtain the source.
- Option A is incorrect because more attempts can't produce information that isn't in the input.
- Option B is incorrect because it encourages the model to guess at values it can't know.
- Option C is incorrect because a fabricated default creates silent data errors.

question: You are building a structured data extraction system for invoices. Source documents sometimes contain internal inconsistencies, such as a stated total that doesn't match the line items, or two different invoice dates. You want the pipeline to detect these cases rather than hide them. Which TWO schema additions support this self-correction flow? (Choose two.)
options: Retry the extraction until the stated total matches the line items.
Extract calculated_total alongside stated_total, so that any discrepancy can be flagged downstream.
Replace the stated total with the sum of the line items whenever the two disagree.
Add a conflict_detected boolean, plus a description, for source data that contradicts itself.
Drop any document whose fields are inconsistent, so that only clean data reaches the system.
explanation:
- Option B is correct because capturing both values makes discrepancies visible and checkable instead of being silently resolved.
- Option D is correct because an explicit conflict flag lets downstream systems or reviewers handle inconsistent sources deliberately.
- Option A is incorrect because if the source itself is inconsistent, retrying can only force the model to misreport it.
- Option C is incorrect because silently overwriting source data hides real billing problems.
- Option E is incorrect because discarding documents loses data and the signal that something needs attention.

question: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline to cut API costs. Currently, real-time Claude calls power two workflows: (1) a blocking pre-merge check that must complete before developers can merge, and (2) a technical debt report generated overnight for review the next morning. Your manager proposes switching both to the Message Batches API for its 50% cost savings. How should you evaluate this proposal?
options: Use batch processing for the technical debt reports only; keep real-time calls for pre-merge checks.
Switch both workflows to batch processing with status polling to check for completion.
Keep real-time calls for both workflows to avoid batch result ordering issues.
Switch both to batch processing with a timeout fallback to real-time if batches take too long.
explanation:
- Option A is correct because the Message Batches API offers 50% cost savings but has processing times up to 24 hours with no guaranteed latency SLA. This makes it unsuitable for blocking pre-merge checks where developers wait for results, but ideal for overnight batch jobs like technical debt reports.
- Option B is incorrect because relying on "often faster" completion isn't acceptable for blocking workflows.
- Option C is incorrect because it reflects a misconception: batch results can be correlated using custom_id fields.
- Option D is incorrect because it adds unnecessary complexity when the simpler solution is matching each API to its appropriate use case.

question: You are building a structured data extraction system. Documents arrive continuously, and the contract guarantees results within 30 hours of arrival. You plan to use the Message Batches API, which can take up to 24 hours to process a batch. How often should you submit batches?
options: Once every 24 hours, matching the batch processing window.
Once every 12 hours, which halves how long documents wait compared with a daily submission.
About every 4 hours, so that the worst case is under 30 hours with margin to spare.
Once a week, to get the most out of the batch discount.
explanation:
- Option C is correct because the worst case is a document that just missed a submission: its wait time equals the submission interval plus up to 24 hours of processing. A 4-hour interval gives at most 28 hours, inside the 30-hour SLA with some margin.
- Option A is incorrect because the worst case is 24 + 24 = 48 hours.
- Option B is incorrect because the worst case is 12 + 24 = 36 hours.
- Option D is incorrect because a weekly cadence breaks the SLA by days; the discount is the same per request whatever the batch size.

question: You are building a structured data extraction system. You submitted a batch of 1,000 documents through the Message Batches API; 962 succeeded and 38 failed because they exceeded the context limit. What should you do next?
options: Resubmit the full batch of 1,000 documents, so that all of the results come from a single run.
Identify the 38 failures by custom_id, chunk those documents into smaller pieces, and resubmit only them.
Resubmit the 38 failed documents exactly as they are, in case the failure was transient.
Move the whole pipeline over to synchronous API calls so that there are no further batch failures to deal with.
explanation:
- Option B is correct because custom_id correlates each request with its result, so you can resubmit only the failures, adjusted for the cause; here that means chunking oversized documents.
- Option A is incorrect because reprocessing 962 successful documents wastes cost and time.
- Option C is incorrect because a context limit failure is deterministic; resubmitting unchanged fails again.
- Option D is incorrect because synchronous calls have the same context limits and double the cost.

question: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline for automated code review. A pull request modifies 14 files across the stock tracking module. Your single-pass review analyzing all files together produces inconsistent results: detailed feedback for some files but superficial comments for others, obvious bugs missed, and contradictory feedback—flagging a pattern as problematic in one file while approving identical code elsewhere in the same PR. How should you restructure the review?
options: Split into focused passes: analyze each file individually for local issues, then run a separate integration-focused pass examining cross-file data flow.
Require developers to split large PRs into smaller submissions of 3-4 files before the automated review runs.
Switch to a higher-tier model with a larger context window to give all 14 files adequate attention in one pass.
Run three independent review passes on the full PR and only flag issues that appear in at least two of the three runs.
explanation:
- Option A is correct because splitting reviews into focused passes directly addresses the root cause: attention dilution when processing many files at once. File-by-file analysis ensures consistent depth, while a separate integration pass catches cross-file issues.
- Option B is incorrect because it shifts the burden to developers without improving the system.
- Option C is incorrect because larger context windows don't solve attention quality issues.
- Option D is incorrect because it would suppress detection of real bugs by requiring consensus on issues that may only be caught intermittently.

question: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. In one job, Claude Code generates a new feature, and then, in the same session, you ask it to "review your changes critically." The review rarely finds anything, yet human reviewers later catch real bugs. What is the most effective improvement?
options: Enable extended thinking for the review step so that the model reasons much more deeply about its own code changes.
Add "Be extremely critical of your own work" to the self-review instruction.
Run the review in a separate, independent Claude instance that has none of the generator's reasoning context.
Ask the generating session to review its changes twice and merge the findings from both passes.
explanation:
- Option C is correct because a model reviewing in the same session keeps the reasoning that led to its decisions and is less likely to question them. An independent instance sees only the code and reviews it fresh.
- Option A is incorrect because extended thinking doesn't remove the bias from shared context.
- Option B is incorrect because a harsher instruction doesn't change what the model already believes about its choices.
- Option D is incorrect because repeating self-review in the same context reproduces the same blind spots.

question: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline for automated review of large PRs. Reviews produce around 40 findings per PR, but the two senior reviewers can verify only about 10. You want to direct their attention where it matters most. What should you add to the review architecture?
options: Report only the first 10 findings in the order the model generated them.
A verification pass where the model reports calibrated confidence with each finding, used to route review attention.
Ask the model to sort its findings alphabetically by file path, so reviewers can work through them in a predictable order.
Ask the model to merge related findings until the total count is at most 10.
explanation:
- Option B is correct because a verification pass with per-finding confidence, calibrated against how past findings turned out, lets you route scarce reviewer time to the findings most likely to matter or most in need of human judgment.
- Option A is incorrect because generation order has no relationship to importance.
- Option C is incorrect because alphabetical ordering ignores both risk and reliability.
- Option D is incorrect because forced merging loses detail and can hide distinct bugs.

question: You are building a customer support resolution agent with the Claude Agent SDK. To fit long conversations into context, older turns are progressively summarized. In a 40-turn billing dispute, the summary reads "Customer was promised a partial refund soon," and the agent later offers the wrong amount. Earlier, the customer had been promised $237.50 by May 3 for order #88213. What is the best fix?
options: Stop summarizing entirely and send the full transcript of every turn with each new request.
Instruct the summarizer to produce longer and more detailed summaries of each turn so that fewer specifics are lost along the way.
Keep amounts, dates, order numbers and statuses in a persistent "case facts" block in every prompt, outside the summary.
Ask the customer to restate any key details whenever the conversation runs longer than 20 turns.
explanation:
- Option C is correct because progressive summarization tends to blur exact numbers, dates and commitments. Keeping a structured facts block outside the summarized history preserves them exactly on every turn.
- Option A is incorrect because it doesn't scale; long conversations will eventually exceed context or dilute attention.
- Option B is incorrect because longer summaries still paraphrase, and precise values remain at risk.
- Option D is incorrect because it pushes the system's memory problem onto the customer and hurts the experience.

question: You are building a customer support resolution agent with the Claude Agent SDK. Each lookup_order call returns more than 40 fields, including warehouse codes, internal SKUs and carrier metadata, but return handling needs only about 5 of them. After several lookups, the context is dominated by irrelevant order data and response quality drops. What should you do?
options: Trim tool outputs to the relevant fields, for example in a PostToolUse hook, before they accumulate in context.
Upgrade to a model with a larger context window so that all of the extra order fields fit in comfortably.
Instruct the agent in the system prompt to disregard any order fields that are not relevant to the return it is handling.
Limit the agent to a single lookup_order call per conversation to keep the context small.
explanation:
- Option A is correct because tool results consume context out of proportion to their relevance. Trimming them to the fields that matter, before they enter the conversation, keeps context focused.
- Option B is incorrect because a larger window delays the problem and doesn't fix the dilution of attention.
- Option C is incorrect because the tokens are still consumed and still compete for attention.
- Option D is incorrect because multi-order cases legitimately need several lookups.

question: You are building a multi-agent research system with the Claude Agent SDK. The synthesis subagent receives results from 12 search and analysis runs concatenated in arrival order. Its reports reliably cover the first and last few results but often omit important findings from the middle. What change best addresses this?
options: Shuffle the order of the results randomly on every run, so that no result is always in the middle.
Send the synthesis agent only the first and last three results, since the middle ones are consistently being ignored anyway.
Repeat every result twice in the input to increase the weight each finding receives.
Lead the input with a summary of key findings and organize the detailed results under explicit section headers.
explanation:
- Option D is correct because models reliably process the beginning and end of long inputs but can miss material in the middle. Leading with a key-findings summary and using clear section headers mitigates this position effect.
- Option A is incorrect because shuffling only changes which findings get lost.
- Option B is incorrect because it deliberately throws away valid findings.
- Option C is incorrect because duplication doubles token use and doesn't fix the positional weakness.

question: You are building a customer support resolution agent with the Claude Agent SDK, using custom MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human) and targeting 80%+ first-contact resolution. Your agent achieves 55% first-contact resolution, well below the 80% target. Logs show it escalates straightforward cases (standard damage replacements with photo evidence) while attempting to autonomously handle complex situations requiring policy exceptions. What's the most effective way to improve escalation calibration?
options: Add explicit escalation criteria to your system prompt with few-shot examples demonstrating when to escalate versus resolve autonomously.
Have the agent self-report a confidence score (1-10) before each response and automatically route requests to humans when confidence falls below a threshold.
Deploy a separate classifier model trained on historical tickets to predict which requests need escalation before the main agent begins processing.
Implement sentiment analysis to detect customer frustration levels and automatically escalate when negative sentiment exceeds a threshold.
explanation:
- Option A is correct because adding explicit escalation criteria with few-shot examples directly addresses the root cause: unclear decision boundaries. This is the proportionate first response before adding infrastructure.
- Option B is incorrect because LLM self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated; the agent is already incorrectly confident on hard cases.
- Option C is incorrect because it is over-engineered, requiring labeled data and ML infrastructure when prompt optimization hasn't been tried.
- Option D is incorrect because it solves a different problem entirely; sentiment doesn't correlate with case complexity, which is the actual issue.

question: You are building a customer support resolution agent with the Claude Agent SDK. A customer's first message is: "I want to talk to a real person, not a bot. My package tracking is wrong." The tracking issue is something the agent can usually resolve in one step. What should the agent do?
options: Look up the tracking information first, then offer to transfer the customer to a human if the answer doesn't satisfy them.
Explain that the agent can resolve tracking issues quickly, and ask the customer to give it a try first.
Honor the request immediately and escalate to a human agent, passing along a structured summary of the issue.
Ask the customer for their reason for wanting a human before deciding whether to escalate.
explanation:
- Option C is correct because an explicit request for a human should be honored immediately, without first attempting investigation. Passing a structured summary means the human doesn't have to start over.
- Option A is incorrect because investigating first overrides the customer's stated preference.
- Option B is incorrect because offering to resolve suits frustration without an explicit request; here the customer has clearly asked for a person.
- Option D is incorrect because customers don't need to justify the request, and questioning them adds friction.

question: You are building a customer support resolution agent with the Claude Agent SDK. Which TWO behaviours reflect correct escalation and ambiguity handling? (Choose two.)
options: A customer asks for a price match against a competitor, but the policy only covers price adjustments on your own site, so the agent escalates.
get_customer returns three accounts matching the customer's name, so the agent picks the most recently active one.
get_customer returns three accounts matching the customer's name, so the agent asks for another identifier, such as an email address or order number.
A customer sounds annoyed about a late delivery but hasn't asked for a human, so the agent escalates based on negative sentiment.
A customer requests a standard damaged-item replacement backed by photo evidence, so the agent escalates because money is involved.
explanation:
- Option A is correct because escalation is appropriate when policy is ambiguous or silent on the customer's specific request, not merely when a case is complex.
- Option C is correct because multiple matches call for clarification with additional identifiers rather than heuristic selection.
- Option B is incorrect because guessing among matching accounts risks acting on the wrong customer.
- Option D is incorrect because sentiment is an unreliable proxy for case complexity; the agent should acknowledge the frustration and resolve the issue, escalating only if the customer asks.
- Option E is incorrect because standard, policy-covered cases should be resolved autonomously to meet first-contact resolution targets.

question: You are building a multi-agent research system with the Claude Agent SDK, in which a coordinator delegates to web search, document analysis, synthesis and report subagents. The web search subagent times out while researching a complex topic. You need to design how this failure information flows back to the coordinator agent. Which error propagation approach best enables intelligent recovery?
options: Return structured error context to the coordinator including the failure type, the attempted query, any partial results, and potential alternative approaches.
Implement automatic retry logic with exponential backoff within the subagent, returning a generic "search unavailable" status only after all retries are exhausted.
Catch the timeout within the subagent and return an empty result set marked as successful.
Propagate the timeout exception directly to a top-level handler that terminates the entire research workflow.
explanation:
- Option A is correct because structured error context gives the coordinator the information it needs to make intelligent recovery decisions: whether to retry with a modified query, try an alternative approach, or proceed with partial results.
- Option B is incorrect because its generic status hides valuable context from the coordinator, preventing informed decisions.
- Option C is incorrect because it suppresses the error by marking failure as success, which prevents any recovery and risks incomplete research outputs.
- Option D is incorrect because it terminates the entire workflow unnecessarily when recovery strategies could succeed.

question: You are building a multi-agent research system with the Claude Agent SDK. The document analysis subagent sometimes receives brief 503 errors from a journal archive, and occasionally the archive is down for hours. Today, every 503 goes straight to the coordinator, which then restarts the whole analysis. What is the best error-handling design?
options: Have the subagent ignore 503 errors and continue, analyzing only the documents it can reach.
Have the coordinator retry the entire analysis from the beginning, up to five times, whenever any subagent error occurs.
Have the subagent retry each request indefinitely until the archive comes back online.
Retry transient failures locally; propagate only unresolved errors with what was attempted and partial results.
explanation:
- Option D is correct because subagents should recover locally from transient failures and escalate only what they can't resolve, along with context. The synthesis can then annotate which areas have gaps because sources were unavailable.
- Option A is incorrect because silently suppressing errors hides the gap from the coordinator and the reader.
- Option B is incorrect because restarting everything discards completed work and repeats it unnecessarily.
- Option C is incorrect because unbounded retries can hang the pipeline for hours.

question: You are building a developer productivity agent with the Claude Agent SDK. Two hours into exploring a legacy codebase, the agent starts answering with phrases like "typically, services like this use a repository pattern" instead of naming the specific OrderRepository and LedgerAdapter classes it found earlier. What technique best counteracts this?
options: Restart the session every 30 minutes no matter how far the exploration has progressed, so that context never grows too large.
Ask the agent to try harder to remember the specific class names it has already found.
Have the agent record key findings in a scratchpad file and consult it for later questions, using /compact as context fills.
Increase max_tokens so the agent has room to write longer and more detailed answers.
explanation:
- Option C is correct because context degrades in extended sessions. A scratchpad file preserves key findings across context boundaries, and /compact reduces bloat from verbose discovery output.
- Option A is incorrect because restarting without a persistence mechanism loses the findings.
- Option B is incorrect because instructions can't restore information the model is no longer attending to reliably.
- Option D is incorrect because output length isn't the problem; the issue is input context degradation.

question: You are building a developer productivity agent with the Claude Agent SDK that coordinates several subagents through a multi-hour codebase analysis. A crash halfway through recently forced the whole analysis to restart. Which TWO design choices improve resilience and keep the coordinator's context manageable? (Choose two.)
options: Have each agent export its state to a known location, and have the coordinator load a manifest on resume and inject that state into agent prompts.
Keep all exploration output in the coordinator's context, so that nothing is lost if a subagent fails.
Restart from scratch after any crash, so that no stale state can carry over into the new run.
Spawn subagents for specific questions, such as "find all test files" or "trace refund flow dependencies", while the coordinator keeps the high-level picture.
Rely on the model remembering the previous session's findings when the analysis restarts.
explanation:
- Option A is correct because structured state exports and a manifest let the coordinator resume exactly where each agent left off.
- Option D is correct because delegating focused investigations isolates verbose output in subagents while the coordinator keeps the overview.
- Option B is incorrect because accumulating everything in one context leads to exhaustion and degraded reasoning.
- Option C is incorrect because it discards hours of valid work.
- Option E is incorrect because a new session has no memory of a previous one unless state is explicitly persisted and injected.

question: You are building a structured data extraction system. It reports 97% field-level accuracy on a validation set, and leadership wants to remove human review for all high-confidence extractions. The validation set is mostly typed PDF invoices, with a small share of scanned handwritten delivery notes. What should you do before reducing human review?
options: Approve the change, since 97% accuracy is well above the threshold the business set.
Raise the confidence threshold for automation from 0.8 to 0.95 first, and then remove the human review step for those extractions.
Analyze accuracy separately by document type and by field to confirm that performance holds across every segment.
Add more typed PDF invoices to the validation set to make the 97% figure more statistically robust.
explanation:
- Option C is correct because aggregate metrics can hide poor performance on specific document types or fields. The handwritten notes could be far less accurate while barely moving the overall number.
- Option A is incorrect because it trusts a figure that may mask a failing segment.
- Option B is incorrect because a stricter threshold doesn't reveal whether confidence is calibrated for each segment.
- Option D is incorrect because it skews the validation set further towards the segment that is already performing well.

question: You are building a structured data extraction system. After calibrating field-level confidence thresholds on a labeled validation set, you now auto-accept high-confidence extractions. How should you keep measuring the error rate of auto-accepted extractions and detect new kinds of errors?
options: Run ongoing stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions across document types for human audit.
Audit only the extractions that downstream users complain about, since those are the cases that matter.
Rely on the model's confidence scores, because high confidence already means the extraction is correct.
Re-run the original validation set once a quarter and compare the latest result with the accuracy baseline you recorded.
explanation:
- Option A is correct because stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions measures the true error rate in each segment and catches novel error patterns that a fixed validation set wouldn't contain.
- Option B is incorrect because complaint-driven audits are biased and miss errors no one notices.
- Option C is incorrect because confidence is a routing signal, not proof of correctness, and calibration can drift.
- Option D is incorrect because a static set can't detect new document formats or error patterns in production traffic.

question: You are building a multi-agent research system with the Claude Agent SDK. Two credible sources report different figures for global e-waste recycled in the same year: 17.4% from a UN report and 22.3% from an industry association. The document analysis subagent currently keeps whichever figure it read first. What should happen instead?
options: Average the two figures and report 19.85% as a single consolidated estimate in the report.
Keep the UN figure, because intergovernmental sources are generally more reliable than industry associations on this kind of question.
Leave both figures out of the report to avoid presenting contested data to readers.
Keep both values with their sources and methodology, and flag the conflict for the coordinator to reconcile before synthesis.
explanation:
- Option D is correct because conflicting statistics from credible sources should be annotated with attribution rather than resolved arbitrarily. Surfacing the conflict lets the coordinator, and ultimately the report, present it as contested.
- Option A is incorrect because averaging invents a number that neither source supports.
- Option B is incorrect because a blanket source-ranking rule discards credible evidence and hides the disagreement.
- Option C is incorrect because omitting the finding removes important, decision-relevant information.

question: You are building a multi-agent research system with the Claude Agent SDK. A synthesis report flags a "contradiction": one source says 45% of firms use AI agents and another says 62%. On inspection, the first figure is from a 2022 survey and the second from 2025. The subagents' outputs didn't include dates. What change prevents this kind of misinterpretation?
options: Instruct the synthesis agent to always assume that the higher figure comes from the more recent source.
Have the synthesis agent discard any statistics that disagree with one another, to keep the report consistent.
Require subagents to output claim-source mappings that include publication or collection dates, which synthesis preserves.
Convert all of the statistics in the report into prose summaries, so that the exact values matter less to the overall conclusions.
explanation:
- Option C is correct because requiring dates and source mappings in structured outputs lets synthesis recognize a trend over time rather than a contradiction, while preserving attribution for every claim.
- Option A is incorrect because the heuristic is unfounded and fails whenever values decrease over time.
- Option B is incorrect because discarding disagreement loses real information, including trends.
- Option D is incorrect because different content types deserve appropriate formats, such as tables for statistics, and vagueness doesn't fix missing dates.

question: You are building a customer support resolution agent with the Claude Agent SDK. Metrics show an average of 4+ API round trips per resolution. Logs reveal that Claude often requests get_customer and lookup_order in separate, sequential turns even though both are needed up front and neither depends on the other's result. What is the most effective way to reduce round trips?
options: Combine get_customer and lookup_order into a single tool that always returns both the customer record and the order details.
Have the loop run every tool_use block in a response and return all results together, and prompt Claude to batch independent lookups.
Pre-fetch the customer and order data before the first model call, using a keyword parser that extracts names and order numbers from the message.
Switch to a faster model tier so that each of the sequential round trips completes in less time.
explanation:
- Option B is correct because Claude can emit several tool_use blocks in one response. A loop that executes all of them and returns every tool_result in the next user message, combined with guidance to batch independent lookups, removes whole round trips without changing the tool design.
- Option A is incorrect because merging unrelated tools blurs their contracts and wastes work when only one lookup is needed.
- Option C is incorrect because a keyword pre-fetcher is brittle post-processing that bypasses the model's understanding of the request.
- Option D is incorrect because it treats the symptom; the number of round trips stays the same.

question: You are building a customer support resolution agent with the Claude Agent SDK. Your loop continues on stop_reason "tool_use" and treats every other stop_reason as a finished answer. Occasionally customers receive replies that stop mid-sentence, and logs show stop_reason "max_tokens" on those turns. What should you change?
options: Add a system prompt instruction asking Claude to keep every reply short enough that it never comes close to the configured token limit.
Detect a truncated-looking reply by checking whether the text ends without punctuation, and regenerate when it does.
Handle "max_tokens" explicitly as a truncated response, for example by raising the limit, and treat only "end_turn" as done.
Lower the iteration cap on the loop so that conversations end before they grow long enough to hit the limit.
explanation:
- Option C is correct because stop_reason distinguishes a finished turn ("end_turn") from a truncated one ("max_tokens"). Each value needs explicit handling; collapsing everything that isn't "tool_use" into "done" ships incomplete answers.
- Option A is incorrect because a prompt instruction is probabilistic and doesn't fix the control-flow bug.
- Option B is incorrect because inspecting text to infer state is the same anti-pattern as parsing natural language for loop control; stop_reason already tells you.
- Option D is incorrect because truncation depends on the length of a single response, not on how many iterations the loop runs.

question: You are building a multi-agent research system with the Claude Agent SDK. A colleague proposes letting the document analysis subagent send its output directly to the synthesis subagent, bypassing the coordinator, to save a step. Which TWO are the strongest reasons to keep all subagent communication routed through the coordinator? (Choose two.)
options: The coordinator gives you one place to observe, log and trace every hand-off between subagents.
Subagents cannot call each other at all, because the SDK has no way for one subagent to reach another.
Routing through the coordinator always lowers total token usage compared with direct hand-offs.
The coordinator can apply consistent error handling and decide what each subagent receives, such as re-delegating when gaps are found.
Direct hand-offs between subagents would automatically share each subagent's full conversation history.
explanation:
- Option A is correct because hub-and-spoke routing gives a single point of observability for debugging and auditing information flow.
- Option D is correct because the coordinator is where error handling, quality checks and iterative refinement decisions are made consistently; direct links scatter that logic across agents.
- Option B is incorrect because the argument is architectural, not a platform limitation.
- Option C is incorrect because an extra hop usually adds tokens; the benefit is control, not cost.
- Option E is incorrect because subagents never share history automatically; context must always be passed explicitly.

question: You are building a multi-agent research system with the Claude Agent SDK. Each subagent is defined with an AgentDefinition. The coordinator often sends document-reading tasks to the web search subagent, whose description is "Research helper," while the document analysis subagent is described as "Helps with research tasks." What is the most effective fix?
options: Rewrite each description to state what the subagent does, the inputs it expects, and when to choose it over the others.
Add a routing table to the coordinator's system prompt that maps keywords such as "PDF" and "search" to the matching subagent names.
Give both subagents the full set of research tools so that it no longer matters which one receives a task.
Replace the coordinator with a deterministic router that sends tasks to subagents based on the file type in the request.
explanation:
- Option A is correct because subagent descriptions play the same role as tool descriptions: they are what the coordinator reads to choose a delegate. Vague, overlapping descriptions cause misrouting at the source.
- Option B is incorrect because keyword routing creates brittle associations and leaves the ambiguous definitions in place.
- Option C is incorrect because giving every agent every tool removes specialization and degrades tool selection.
- Option D is incorrect because a rigid router can't handle requests that don't fit file-type rules and discards model-driven delegation.

question: You are building a developer productivity agent with the Claude Agent SDK. To add your team's conventions, a teammate set systemPrompt to a custom string containing only those conventions. Since then the agent uses its tools less effectively and has dropped behaviours it used to follow, such as asking before destructive operations. What is the best fix?
options: Copy the full Claude Code system prompt text into your custom string, then add the team's conventions at the end of it.
Use the claude_code preset with append set to the team's conventions, so the defaults are extended rather than replaced.
Move the conventions into a PostToolUse hook that injects them into each tool result the agent receives.
Leave systemPrompt unset so the SDK falls back to its built-in defaults, and paste the team conventions into each user prompt instead.
explanation:
- Option B is correct because a custom systemPrompt string replaces the default prompt, removing its tool guidance and safety instructions. The claude_code preset with append keeps all of that and adds your instructions after it, which makes it the lowest-risk customization.
- Option A is incorrect because a hand-copied prompt goes stale as the preset evolves.
- Option C is incorrect because hooks are for deterministic interception, not for carrying standing instructions.
- Option D is incorrect because an unset systemPrompt gives a minimal prompt, not the Claude Code preset, and repeating conventions in every user message is fragile.

question: You are building a customer support resolution agent with the Claude Agent SDK. The cancel_subscription tool has a dry_run boolean so the agent can preview the impact, such as lost credits and the final invoice, and the customer can confirm. Monitoring shows the agent sometimes calls it with dry_run=false straight away, skipping both the preview and the confirmation. How should you guarantee a confirmed preview before every cancellation?
options: Add a bold system prompt rule stating that cancel_subscription must always be called with dry_run=true first.
Add few-shot examples that show the agent previewing the impact, asking the customer to confirm, and only then cancelling the subscription.
Have the agent self-report whether the customer confirmed, and cancel only when it reports that they did.
Split it into preview_cancellation, which issues a token, and execute_cancellation, which code rejects without a customer-confirmed token.
explanation:
- Option D is correct because ordering requirements with real consequences should be enforced programmatically. Making the executing tool depend on a token issued by the preview step, and checked in code, makes skipping the preview impossible.
- Option A is incorrect because prompt instructions have a non-zero failure rate, which is exactly what monitoring shows.
- Option B is incorrect because examples raise the odds of compliance but can't guarantee it.
- Option C is incorrect because self-reported state is not verification; the model can be wrong about what happened.

question: You are building a developer productivity agent with the Claude Agent SDK that uses Bash. Engineers run it against laptops that also hold production credentials, and policy says the agent must never run commands that target the production cluster, such as kubectl with the prod context. What is the most reliable way to enforce this?
options: A PreToolUse hook that blocks any Bash command targeting the production context and returns the reason to the agent.
A system prompt rule, repeated in CLAUDE.md, that forbids any command which targets the production cluster.
A post-session audit script that scans the Bash history and alerts security when a production command has run.
Removing Bash from the agent's tools entirely, so that it can no longer run any shell commands on the engineer's laptop at all.
explanation:
- Option A is correct because tool call interception hooks enforce policy deterministically before the action runs, and returning a reason lets the agent explain the block and choose an alternative.
- Option B is incorrect because prompt guidance gives probabilistic compliance, which isn't acceptable for production safety.
- Option C is incorrect because detection after the fact doesn't prevent the damage.
- Option D is incorrect because it removes legitimate, high-value capability to address a narrow risk that a hook can target precisely.

question: Your team uses Claude Code for refactoring. A developer spent yesterday analyzing a 40-file billing module in a named session. Overnight a teammate changed two of those files: invoice_totals.py and tax_rules.py. Everything else is unchanged. What is the most efficient way to continue?
options: Resume the named session and tell Claude exactly which two files changed, so it re-reads and re-analyzes only those.
Start a fresh session and re-run the full analysis, so that no stale context from yesterday is carried forward.
Fork yesterday's session and continue the work in the fork, leaving the original session untouched as a backup.
Resume the named session without mentioning the changes, since Claude will re-read any file it needs to touch during the work anyway.
explanation:
- Option A is correct because when prior context is mostly valid, resuming is efficient, and naming the specific changed files lets Claude refresh only what is stale.
- Option B is incorrect because discarding a mostly valid analysis wastes time; a fresh start with a summary is for when most prior results are stale.
- Option C is incorrect because a fork inherits the same unflagged stale results for the two changed files.
- Option D is incorrect because Claude can keep reasoning from the earlier contents of the changed files without re-reading them.

question: You are building a multi-agent research system with the Claude Agent SDK. The web search subagent queried three source categories: academic databases returned 15 papers, industry reports returned zero matches, and the patent database timed out. How should it report these outcomes to the coordinator?
options: Report the 15 papers and mark the task as successful, since at least one of the source categories produced results.
Report a single error for the whole search, since one category failed and the overall result is therefore unreliable.
Report the papers as results, industry reports as a successful query with no matches, and the patent timeout as a retryable failure.
Report all three outcomes as free-text notes in the response, so that the coordinator can work out what happened from the descriptions.
explanation:
- Option C is correct because valid empty results and access failures mean different things. "No matches" is information, while a timeout needs a retry or an alternative, so each outcome should be reported as such with structured status.
- Option A is incorrect because it hides the patent failure, so the coordinator can't recover and the report silently loses coverage.
- Option B is incorrect because it throws away good results and forces unnecessary rework.
- Option D is incorrect because unstructured notes make the coordinator infer status, which leads to inconsistent recovery decisions.

question: You are building a developer productivity agent with the Claude Agent SDK. It connects to six MCP servers that expose 90 tools between them, and the tool definitions alone consume about 40,000 tokens on every request. Costs have risen, and long tasks degrade as they approach the context limit. What is the most effective change?
options: Move to a model with a larger context window so that the tool definitions take up a smaller share of the available space.
Cut every tool description down to a single short sentence so that the 90 definitions consume far fewer tokens.
Cache the tool definitions on the client side so that they are sent with the first request only.
Scope MCP servers and tools to each agent's role, so that each agent or subagent loads only the tools its work needs.
explanation:
- Option D is correct because tool definitions are part of the context budget on every request. Scoping tools by role cuts that fixed cost and also improves tool selection, which degrades as the tool count grows.
- Option A is incorrect because a bigger window raises the ceiling but keeps paying for irrelevant definitions, and dilution remains.
- Option B is incorrect because terse descriptions make tool selection worse; descriptions are how the model tells tools apart.
- Option C is incorrect because the model needs the definitions in context to call the tools; they can't be dropped from later requests.

question: You are building a developer productivity agent with the Claude Agent SDK. You connected an MCP server whose find_symbol tool resolves definitions and references across the monorepo, including generated code. The agent still uses Grep for almost every lookup and misses references in generated files. The find_symbol description reads "Finds symbols." What should you do first?
options: Expand the description to explain what find_symbol resolves that Grep misses, plus its inputs and output format.
Remove Grep from the agent's tools so that it has no choice but to use find_symbol for every lookup.
Add a system prompt rule telling the agent to always prefer MCP tools over the built-in tools wherever both of them could do the job.
Rename the tool to grep_symbols so that it is more strongly associated with search in the model's mind.
explanation:
- Option A is correct because agents choose tools from their descriptions. A one-line description gives the model no reason to prefer the MCP tool over a familiar built-in, while a detailed one makes its advantages explicit.
- Option B is incorrect because Grep is still the right tool for plain text searches, such as error messages.
- Option C is incorrect because a blanket preference rule ignores which tool fits each task and leaves the weak description in place.
- Option D is incorrect because a misleading name invites confusion with Grep rather than explaining the difference.

question: Your team uses Claude Code and wants it to read and update Jira tickets. One engineer proposes building a custom MCP server for Jira. A maintained community Jira MCP server already covers search, comments and transitions. Separately, the team has a bespoke release-approval workflow that exists only in an internal service. What is the best approach?
options: Build one custom MCP server that covers both Jira and the release-approval workflow, so the team owns all of its integrations.
Use the community Jira MCP server, and build a custom MCP server only for the team-specific release-approval workflow.
Skip MCP entirely and have Claude call the Jira and approval APIs with curl through the Bash tool.
Use the community Jira server, and handle release approvals by documenting the API endpoints in CLAUDE.md.
explanation:
- Option B is correct because standard integrations are best served by existing community servers, which saves build and maintenance effort. Custom servers are reserved for workflows unique to the team.
- Option A is incorrect because rebuilding a well-supported integration adds ongoing cost with no benefit.
- Option C is incorrect because ad hoc shell calls give up typed tool interfaces, clear descriptions and structured errors.
- Option D is incorrect because documentation is not a tool; Claude would still need a dependable way to perform the approval actions.

question: You are building a developer productivity agent with the Claude Agent SDK. An engineer asks it to find every caller of formatCurrency. Grep finds only three call sites, but the function is re-exported from utils/index.ts as both formatMoney and fmt, which most modules import. What approach finds every usage?
options: Read every file that imports from utils/ and look through each one for currency formatting by hand.
Grep for the word "currency" across the whole repository and report every one of the matches that the search returns.
Use Glob to list every TypeScript file in the repository, then Read each of those files in turn.
First identify all the names the wrapper module exports for the function, then Grep for each of those names.
explanation:
- Option D is correct because tracing usage through wrapper modules means finding every alias first, then searching for each one. This stays targeted and complete.
- Option A is incorrect because reading many files by hand is slow and context-hungry, and still error-prone.
- Option B is incorrect because a loose keyword search returns noise and misses calls through aliases such as fmt.
- Option C is incorrect because reading the whole codebase exhausts context; Glob finds file names, not call sites.

question: You are building a customer support resolution agent with the Claude Agent SDK. Tool descriptions are clear, but the agent still mis-routes ambiguous messages such as "I need help with my recent purchase," which could call for get_customer or lookup_order. You decide to add few-shot examples. Which kind of examples will help most?
options: Fifteen straightforward examples, such as "check order #123" leading to lookup_order, covering each tool in turn.
Examples that list every possible user phrasing next to the tool it should map to.
2-4 examples of ambiguous requests, each showing the reasoning for choosing one tool over the plausible alternative.
A single example of the ideal full conversation, from the customer's greeting all the way through to the final resolution.
explanation:
- Option C is correct because targeted examples of ambiguous cases, with reasoning about why one option beats another, teach the judgment the model lacks and let it generalize to new phrasings.
- Option A is incorrect because clear-cut cases are already handled; more of them add tokens without addressing the ambiguity.
- Option B is incorrect because exhaustive mappings can't cover real-world variety and turn judgment into lookup.
- Option D is incorrect because one end-to-end transcript doesn't isolate the decision that is going wrong.

question: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. To make the reviewer focus on security, the job runs claude -p --system-prompt "You are a strict security reviewer. Report only vulnerabilities." Since then reviews have become shallower, and Claude no longer follows its usual tool-use and file-handling behaviour. What is the best fix?
options: Use --append-system-prompt for the security instructions, so they extend the default system prompt instead of replacing it.
Lengthen the --system-prompt text until it also covers tool usage, file handling and all of the safety guidance in full detail.
Move the security focus into the -p prompt text, and keep --system-prompt with a short, generic reviewer role description.
Add the security focus to CLAUDE.md, and keep --system-prompt as it is for reinforcement.
explanation:
- Option A is correct because --system-prompt replaces the entire default system prompt, while --append-system-prompt adds instructions after it. Appending keeps Claude Code's built-in behaviour and adds the review focus, which is the safer way to customize at runtime.
- Option B is incorrect because hand-maintaining a copy of the default prompt is fragile and drifts as Claude Code changes.
- Option C is incorrect because any --system-prompt value, however short, still replaces the default system prompt, so the built-in behaviour stays lost.
- Option D is incorrect because keeping --system-prompt still discards the default prompt; CLAUDE.md doesn't restore it.

question: Your team runs a test-generation job built on the Claude Agent SDK in CI. To stop CI from picking up developers' personal settings, someone set settingSources: ["user"]. Since then, generated tests ignore the fixture conventions and testing standards documented in the repository's CLAUDE.md. What is the cause and the fix?
options: The CLAUDE.md file is too long for the SDK to load, so it should be split into several smaller files.
CLAUDE.md is loaded only by the claude_code system prompt preset, so the job needs to switch to that preset to pick up the conventions.
The project setting source is missing; use settingSources: ["project"] to load the repo's CLAUDE.md without user settings.
CLAUDE.md applies only in interactive sessions, so the conventions should be pasted into the job's prompt instead.
explanation:
- Option C is correct because the SDK loads CLAUDE.md through setting sources: "project" loads the repository's CLAUDE.md and "user" loads ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. Listing only "user" accidentally dropped the project context, and switching to ["project"] keeps the team context while excluding personal settings.
- Option A is incorrect because length isn't the issue; the file isn't being loaded at all.
- Option B is incorrect because CLAUDE.md loading is controlled by setting sources, not by the system prompt preset.
- Option D is incorrect because CLAUDE.md is the intended way to give project context to CI-invoked Claude.

question: Your team uses Claude Code for code generation. Including 2-3 complete reference implementations of API endpoints markedly improves consistency when generating new endpoints. That material runs to about 3,000 tokens and is irrelevant when debugging, reviewing or writing documentation. Where should it live?
options: In a project skill under .claude/skills/, which developers invoke when they create a new endpoint.
In the root CLAUDE.md, so that the examples are always available whenever they might be needed.
In each developer's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, so that it doesn't clutter the shared project configuration.
In a .claude/rules/ file scoped to every file in the repository, so that it loads automatically.
explanation:
- Option A is correct because skills are loaded on demand for specific tasks, while CLAUDE.md holds always-loaded universal standards. Task-specific reference material belongs in a skill.
- Option B is incorrect because it spends 3,000 tokens of context in every session, including the many that never create endpoints.
- Option C is incorrect because it has the same always-loaded cost and isn't shared with the team.
- Option D is incorrect because a rule matching every file is effectively always loaded, which defeats path scoping.

question: Your team uses Claude Code and shares a /commit skill in .claude/skills/commit/SKILL.md. One developer wants a variant with a different message format and extra pre-commit checks for personal use, without changing what teammates get. What should they do?
options: Edit the shared SKILL.md and add a condition that applies the extra checks only when their username is detected.
Create a personal skill in ~/.claude/skills/ with a different name, such as /my-commit, containing their variant.
Create ~/.claude/skills/commit/SKILL.md with the same name, so that their personal version overrides the team skill.
Put the variant's instructions in their ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md so that they apply whenever they commit.
explanation:
- Option B is correct because personal variants belong in ~/.claude/skills/ under a distinct name. This leaves the team skill untouched and avoids any ambiguity about which version runs.
- Option A is incorrect because user-specific logic in a shared skill complicates it for everyone.
- Option C is incorrect because reusing the same name invites confusion about which skill runs; a distinct name is the safe pattern.
- Option D is incorrect because always-loaded memory isn't the place for an on-demand workflow.

question: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline for test generation. For a PR that adds course-completion tracking, Claude suggested 10 test cases, and developers found that 6 duplicated scenarios already covered by the existing suite. What change most effectively reduces duplicate suggestions?
options: Ask Claude to suggest fewer test cases per PR, so that a smaller share of its suggestions turn out to be duplicates.
Add a post-processing step that compares suggested test names against existing test names and removes any suggestions that match.
Run test generation with a larger model, which is better at guessing what the existing suite already covers.
Include the relevant existing test files in context, and document the testing standards and available fixtures in CLAUDE.md.
explanation:
- Option D is correct because Claude can only avoid duplicating tests it can see. Giving it the existing tests, plus documented standards and fixtures, addresses the root cause upstream and improves the quality of what it does suggest.
- Option A is incorrect because it reduces valuable suggestions along with the duplicates.
- Option B is incorrect because name matching misses duplicates with different names and is brittle post-processing.
- Option C is incorrect because no model can infer coverage it hasn't been shown.

question: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The PR reviewer job should be able to read and search the code but must never edit files or run shell commands. A teammate configured claude -p --allowedTools "Read,Grep,Glob" and believes that restricts the tools. Which configuration actually limits the available built-in tools?
options: --allowedTools "Read,Grep,Glob", because listing tools there is exactly what makes every other tool unavailable to the session.
A CLAUDE.md instruction telling Claude never to use the Edit, Write or Bash tools during review.
--tools "Read,Grep,Glob", which restricts the built-in tool set, optionally with --disallowedTools for anything else to deny.
--append-system-prompt "Only read files", which tells the model to stay within read-only behaviour.
explanation:
- Option C is correct because --tools defines which built-in tools are available, and --disallowedTools removes or denies tools. Deterministic configuration beats instructions when a capability must be unavailable.
- Option A is incorrect because --allowedTools pre-approves the listed tools so they run without a permission prompt; it doesn't restrict Claude to them.
- Option B is incorrect because instructions in CLAUDE.md are guidance, not enforcement.
- Option D is incorrect because a prompt instruction still leaves the tools available.

question: You are building a structured data extraction system. Incoming documents are invoices, receipts or purchase orders, and you have defined a separate extraction tool with its own JSON schema for each. The type isn't known in advance, and the model sometimes replies with a prose description instead of calling any tool. How should you configure tool_choice?
options: tool_choice: "auto", with a system prompt instruction telling Claude that it must call one of the three tools.
tool_choice: "any", so that Claude must call a tool but chooses the schema that fits the document.
Force tool_choice to the invoice tool for every document, and let the model leave irrelevant fields empty.
Run all three tools on every document and keep whichever output has the fewest empty fields.
explanation:
- Option B is correct because "any" guarantees a tool call, and therefore structured output, while letting the model pick the right schema for an unknown document type.
- Option A is incorrect because "auto" allows a text reply, which is the failure you are seeing.
- Option C is incorrect because forcing a single schema mis-structures receipts and purchase orders and encourages fabricated fields.
- Option D is incorrect because running every extractor triples the cost, and "fewest empty fields" rewards hallucination.

question: You are building a structured data extraction system for invoices. Extraction uses tool_use with a schema that declares invoice_date as a string, and source invoices write dates as "03/04/25", "4 March 2025" and "2025-03-04". Downstream systems receive this mix and misread day and month. What is the best fix?
options: Describe the field as an ISO 8601 date in the schema, and add prompt rules for reading day/month order by supplier region.
Add a regex post-processor after extraction that detects each of the date formats and rewrites the value as an ISO 8601 date.
Ask a second Claude call to clean up the dates after the extraction has already finished.
Make invoice_date an enum covering the date formats you have seen so far, so that the model must choose one.
explanation:
- Option A is correct because combining a precise schema with explicit normalization rules fixes the problem where the value is produced. The model has the document's context, such as the supplier's locale, to resolve ambiguous dates, which a downstream patch doesn't.
- Option B is incorrect because regex post-processing can't tell whether "03/04/25" means 3 April or 4 March; it guesses and silently corrupts data.
- Option C is incorrect because a second pass adds cost and latency and has lost the original document context.
- Option D is incorrect because an enum of formats doesn't normalize the value and breaks on the next new format.

question: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline for automated review. The same null-pointer risk is rated "critical" in some PRs and "medium" in others, and developers have started ignoring severity altogether. The prompt currently says "Rate each finding as critical, high, medium or low." What change best fixes the inconsistency?
options: Lower the temperature to 0 so that the same code always receives the same severity rating.
Define explicit criteria for each severity level, each with a concrete code example of a finding at that level.
Ask the model to rate every finding twice and then average the two ratings, smoothing out the variation between PRs.
Remove severity ratings entirely and let developers prioritize the findings themselves.
explanation:
- Option B is correct because explicit, example-anchored severity definitions give the model a stable rubric, which is what produces consistent classification across PRs.
- Option A is incorrect because determinism without a rubric just makes the same arbitrary choice repeatedly; different PRs will still differ.
- Option C is incorrect because averaging two undefined judgments doesn't create a definition.
- Option D is incorrect because it throws away useful prioritization rather than fixing it.

question: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline for automated review. Developers dismiss about 30% of findings, but you can't tell which kinds of code trigger the dismissed findings, so you don't know which criteria to improve. What should you add to the structured findings?
options: A free-text "reasoning" field on each finding, which reviewers can read through when they are deciding whether to dismiss it.
A field recording the time at which the developer dismissed the finding, to help track how quickly reviews happen.
A detected_pattern field naming the code construct that triggered each finding, so dismissals can be analyzed by pattern.
A field holding the model's self-assessed confidence, so that findings below a threshold are hidden automatically.
explanation:
- Option C is correct because recording which construct triggered each finding turns dismissals into data. You can see, for example, that most dismissed findings are about early returns in validators, and fix those specific criteria.
- Option A is incorrect because free text is hard to aggregate across thousands of findings.
- Option B is incorrect because timing data doesn't explain why findings are wrong.
- Option D is incorrect because hiding findings by uncalibrated confidence hides the problem instead of diagnosing it.

question: You are building a structured data extraction system for logistics documents. The model sometimes puts the order date into ship_date because the two appear near each other, and when no ship date is stated it fills ship_date with the order date. Which TWO changes address the root cause most directly? (Choose two.)
options: Upgrade to the highest model tier, since better models make fewer mistakes of this kind.
Add contrastive few-shot examples pairing near-miss cases, such as an order date beside a ship date, with the correct extraction for each.
Raise max_tokens so that the model has room to reason more carefully about each field.
Add an explicit abstention instruction, with ship_date nullable, stating that null is the correct answer when no ship date is given.
Add a regex check that rejects any extraction where ship_date equals order_date.
explanation:
- Option B is correct because contrastive examples show the model exactly where the boundary between two similar fields lies, which is the semantic nuance it is getting wrong.
- Option D is correct because an explicit abstention path, with a nullable field and an instruction that null is correct, removes the pressure to fill the field with a plausible but wrong value.
- Option A is incorrect because jumping to a bigger model is rarely the targeted fix for a specification gap; the same ambiguity remains.
